title: Allow One Function Call
statement:
Write `once(fn)`, which returns a wrapper around `fn` that lets `fn` run **at most one time**. The first call of the wrapper passes its arguments to `fn` and returns whatever `fn` gives back. Every later call returns `undefined` and does not call `fn` at all.

In this kit `fn` is one of four functions of any number of arguments: `"sum"` adds them, `"product"` multiplies them, `"max"` returns the largest and `"min"` the smallest.

Each case gives the name `fn` and `calls`, a list of argument lists: the wrapper is called once with each list, in order. The answer lists every call of the wrapper that returned something other than `undefined` or made `fn` run, each as `{ calls, value }`: `calls` is how many times `fn` has run so far in total, and `value` is what the wrapper returned (`null` for `undefined`).
constraints: calls[i][j] is an integer from -1000 to 1000
For "product", the product of every calls[i] is at most 10^15 in absolute value
api: once(fn: (...args: number[]) => number): (...args: number[]) => number | undefined
notes:
## Intuition

The wrapper has to remember whether `fn` already ran, and that memory must outlive each call. A variable declared in `once` and read by the returned function is exactly that: a closure. One boolean flag is enough. The brute force counts calls instead and runs `fn` only when the count is 1, which is the same idea with a number.

## Approach

1. Create `called = false` inside `once`, so every wrapper gets its own flag.
2. Return a function that takes any arguments as `args`.
3. If `called` is already true, return `undefined` without touching `fn`.
4. Otherwise set `called = true` first, then return `fn(...args)`.

## Example 1, step by step

`fn` is `"sum"` and `calls = [[1,2,3],[2,3,6]]`.

- First call with `(1, 2, 3)`: `called` is false, so it becomes true and `fn` runs, returning `6`. `fn` has run once, so the answer gets `{ calls: 1, value: 6 }`.
- Second call with `(2, 3, 6)`: `called` is true, so the wrapper returns `undefined` and `fn` does not run. Nothing is added.
- The answer is `[{ calls: 1, value: 6 }]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) per call besides the single run of `fn`.
- Space: O(1): one flag per wrapper.

## Pitfalls

- Deciding "already ran" from the stored result, as in `if (!result)`, runs `fn` again whenever its first result is `0` (see a product with a zero).
- Putting the flag outside `once` makes all wrappers share it, so the second wrapper never runs its `fn`.
- Forgetting to spread the arguments: `fn(args)` passes one array instead of the separate values.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `fn` | the function allowed to run once |
| `called` | whether `fn` has already run for this wrapper |
| `args` | the arguments of the current call of the wrapper |

narration.1: once runs a single time per wrapper and sets up its private state.
narration.2: called is the closure flag that records whether fn has run yet.
narration.3: Every call of the wrapper arrives here with its arguments.
narration.4: If fn already ran, this call must not run it again.
narration.5: Later calls give back undefined and leave fn alone.
narration.7: Mark the flag before running fn, so no later call gets through.
narration.8: The first call runs fn with the same arguments and returns its result.
